HeMeR: Heterogeneous Memory Reconciliation for Embodied Agents via Structured KV Reuse

Saehun Chun Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University Email: thousae@skku.edu    Wonje Choi Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University Email: wjchoi1995@skku.edu    Jinwoo Jang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University Email: jinustar@skku.edu    Taeyoon Kwack Affiliation: Department of Artificial Intelligence, Sungkyunkwan University Email: njj05043@skku.edu    Honguk Woo ††thanks: Honguk Woo is the corresponding author. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University Affiliation: Department of Artificial Intelligence, Sungkyunkwan University Email: hwoo@skku.edu
Abstract

Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent’s state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20%83.20\% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.942.94 to 1.871.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.

1 Introduction

Embodied agents increasingly build on foundation models, using language or vision-language models to interpret observations, reason about goals, and select actions [1, base:react, embodied:llmplanner, 13, embodied:progprompt, embodied:voyager]. However, embodied tasks often require information beyond immediate observations, including explicit environmental knowledge, learned behavioral routines, and ongoing task progress [13, embodied:progprompt, embodied:voyager, embodied:reflexion]. Accordingly, recent studies augment foundation models with memory modules that store, retrieve, and update task-relevant memory contents across interactions [embodied:voyager, embodied:reflexion, method:genagent, serve:memgpt, mem:memorybank]. These modules help agents preserve continuity over long-horizon tasks, but also make each action decision depend on memory contents that change with accumulated experience, current observations, and task progress.

Recent memory-augmented agents use heterogeneous memory modules that maintain distinct forms of memory content for embodied decision making [base:react, embodied:voyager, method:genagent, embodied:coala]. A declarative memory module maintains explicit content about environmental objects, relations, and task conditions, often as structured representations such as symbolic facts [method:genagent, serve:memgpt, mem:amem, 7]. A procedural memory module maintains learned behavioral routines that guide future actions [embodied:progprompt, embodied:voyager, mem:procedural, 6], including parametric representations such as neural adapters [11]. A working memory module maintains content about the current task state, including recent observations, intermediate decisions, and goal progress [base:react, 13, mem:working]. Although these modules are often studied through separate storage, retrieval, and update mechanisms, action selection requires their contents to be composed into a memory context. The resulting memory context is processed by the foundation model to form transformer KV states during inference [mem:kv, serve:vllm]. As the agent receives new observations and progresses through the task, the memory context must be updated while many memory contents remain unchanged across consecutive decisions.

This modular separation is well motivated, since each memory module serves a distinct role in embodied decision making [embodied:coala, mem:procedural, mem:working, mem:episodic]. However, after memory contents from multiple memory modules are composed into a single memory context, the foundation model must process this memory context to form the hidden representations and KV states used for action selection [mem:kv, serve:vllm]. As illustrated in Figure 1, changes in the environment can trigger updates to declarative and working memory contents and procedural adapter switches, thereby changing the memory context across decision steps. Such changes can make some previously cached KV states incompatible with the updated memory context, while others may remain reusable [serve:cacheblend, serve:kvlink, serve:cacheslide, pos:rope, 14, 15]. Existing memory-augmented agents mainly focus on what to store, retrieve, and update, but do not explicitly address how to reconcile updated memory contexts with reusable KV states during foundation model inference [serve:memgpt, mem:memorybank, mem:amem, 16, mem:titans]. Without such reconciliation, a naive implementation processes each updated memory context as a new input and recomputes the full KV cache, causing redundant computation during long-horizon embodied interaction [serve:kvlink, 12, 17, 5].

To address this problem, we introduce HeMeR, a memory-serving framework for embodied agents that reconciles dynamically updated memory contexts with reusable KV states during foundation model inference. Although declarative, procedural, and working memory serve different roles, their effects on foundation model inference are ultimately reflected in the KV states used for action selection. Rather than treating each memory context as a flat token sequence, HeMeR represents it as a sequence of structured memory chunks associated with corresponding KV ranges, providing a common basis for reconciling heterogeneous memory updates with cached KV states. HeMeR realizes this reconciliation through two complementary mechanisms, Chunk-Level KV Reconciliation for content-level changes and rearrangements within the memory context, and Adapter-Stable KV Reconciliation for procedural changes that alter the active adapter.

Specifically, Chunk-Level KV Reconciliation handles updates to declarative and working memory contents by mapping content-level changes and rearrangements to their corresponding KV ranges. HeMeR identifies reusable KV ranges by tracking changes in memory contents and their dependencies, selectively recomputing only the affected ranges. When an unchanged memory chunk shifts position, RoPE-based remapping preserves positional consistency, allowing its KV states to be reused [pos:rope]. Adapter-Stable KV Reconciliation handles procedural memory updates that alter the active adapter. Because KV states computed under a previous adapter may become incompatible even when other memory contents remain unchanged, HeMeR treats the adapter configuration as part of the KV compatibility condition, selectively recomputing affected KV ranges while preserving compatible KV states across adapter switches. By jointly reconciling memory content updates and procedural adapter changes without rebuilding the full KV cache, HeMeR supports efficient and stable inference over long-horizon embodied tasks.

We evaluate HeMeR on unseen simulated tasks from ALFWorld [19] and EmbodiedBench Habitat [ben:embodiedbench, 20], where evaluation episodes require the agent to combine memory contents across different situations rather than rely on a directly applicable memory content. We further evaluate HeMeR on real-world embodied tasks in a UR7e manipulation setup, requiring the agent to coordinate heterogeneous memory contents as procedures and task states change. We highlight task success rate and inference time per decision step, with each step corresponding to one action selection. On ALFWorld, HeMeR achieves a 71.43%71.43\% task success rate with 0.180.18 seconds per decision step, compared with a 52.86%52.86\% task success rate and 0.900.90 seconds per decision step for MemRL [26], the strongest baseline in task success (Table 1). On EmbodiedBench Habitat, HeMeR achieves a 76.27%76.27\% task success rate with 1.821.82 seconds per decision step, compared with a 61.80%61.80\% task success rate and 2.682.68 seconds per decision step for MemRL (Table 1). In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves an 83.20% goal-conditioned success rate with 1.87 seconds per decision step, compared with a 64.28% goal-conditioned success rate and 2.94 seconds per decision step for MemRL (Table 2). These results show that KV reconciliation improves task robustness and inference efficiency as memory contexts change across embodied decision steps.

We make the following contributions.

  • •

    We formulate heterogeneous memory use as a KV reconciliation problem for foundation model-based embodied agents, where memory contents from declarative, procedural, and working memory modules change across action decisions while many contents remain reusable.

  • •

    We introduce HeMeR, a heterogeneous memory reconciliation framework that anchors memory contents as typed chunks with KV ranges and selectively reuses compatible KV states.

  • •

    We develop chunk-level and adapter-stable KV reconciliation mechanisms that update only affected KV ranges, preserve positional consistency under memory-content updates, and maintain compatible KV states across procedural adapter switches.

  • •

    We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments, showing that it improves task success and reduces per-step inference time over strong baselines.

2 Related work

Foundation Model-based Embodied Control.

Recent studies use language and vision-language foundation models as general-purpose decision modules for embodied agents, enabling them to interpret observations, reason about goals, and select actions in interactive environments [1, embodied:llmplanner, 13, embodied:progprompt, embodied:voyager, embodied:ecot]. These agents are further augmented with memory modules to store and retrieve task-relevant memory contents across decision steps and adapt action selection over long-horizon interactions [embodied:reflexion, mem:memorybank, 28, 26, 21]. HeMeR follows this line of work, but focuses on the inference problem that arises when memory contents from multiple memory modules are composed into a dynamically updated memory context that must be reconciled with reusable KV states across action decisions.

Memory-Augmented Embodied Agents.

Recent memory-augmented embodied agents introduce specialized memory modules for different roles in decision making. Declarative memory modules maintain explicit content about environmental objects, relations, and task conditions [method:genagent, mem:memorybank, mem:amem, 7]. Procedural memory modules maintain learned behavioral routines, including reusable procedures and skills [embodied:progprompt, embodied:voyager, mem:procedural, 6, 10, mem:automanual, 24, 14]. Working memory modules maintain memory content about recent observations, intermediate decisions, and goal progress during the current interaction [base:react, 13, embodied:coala, mem:working]. These memory modules help embodied agents preserve task-relevant memory content beyond immediate observations and adapt action selection over time. However, existing studies mainly focus on how each memory module stores, retrieves, or updates its own memory content for a role-specific objective. In contrast, HeMeR jointly handles memory contents from declarative, procedural, and working memory modules once they are composed into a single memory context, reconciling their updates with reusable KV states across action decisions.

Efficient KV Reuse.

KV caching is a standard mechanism for efficient autoregressive inference, in which previously computed KV states are stored and reused across decoding steps [mem:kv, serve:vllm, serve:orca]. Prior work on KV reuse reduces inference cost by reusing cached KV states for repeated prefixes, shared prompts, or recurring context segments [12, kv:promptcache, 8]. Recent systems further exploit structured generation programs, retrieved context chunks, position-independent context segments, or embodied reasoning traces to reuse computation across related inference requests or decision steps [serve:cacheblend, serve:kvlink, serve:cacheslide, serve:sglang, 9, 23]. Complementary work reduces KV cache storage requirements, transfer costs, or loading overhead through eviction, compression, streaming, or cache-layer management [17, 5, 27, 22]. In parallel, multi-adapter serving systems improve the efficiency of models augmented with LoRA adapters by batching requests, switching adapters, or reusing KV states across adapters during inference [11, 14, 15, serve:slora, serve:punica, serve:dlora, 25]. Building on these advances, HeMeR integrates KV reuse and multi-adapter serving techniques within a memory-serving framework to efficiently reuse KV states as memory contexts change across action decisions.

3 Problem formulation

We consider a foundation model-based embodied agent that acts over a sequence of decision steps. At step tt, the agent receives an observation oto_{t}, maintains a task goal gg, and selects an action ata_{t} using a foundation model FθF_{\theta}. The agent is augmented with heterogeneous memory modules

ℳ={ℳdec,ℳproc,ℳwork},\mathcal{M}=\{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{dec}},\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{proc}},\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{work}}\}, (1)

corresponding to declarative, procedural, and working memory modules. A memory module stores and retrieves information, and each item it returns is a memory content. For each module ℳm\mathcal{M}^{m}, let RmR^{m} denote its retrieval function and ℛtm\mathcal{R}_{t}^{m} the memory contents obtained at step tt:

ℛtm=Rm​(ot,g,ht),m∈{dec,proc,work}.\mathcal{R}_{t}^{m}=R^{m}(o_{t},g,h_{t}),\quad m\in\{\mathrm{dec},\mathrm{proc},\mathrm{work}\}. (2)

Here, hth_{t} denotes the interaction history available at step tt.

For readability, we denote the declarative, procedural, and working-memory contents as

Dt=ℛtdec,Pt=ℛtproc,Wt=ℛtwork.D_{t}=\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{dec}},\quad P_{t}=\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{proc}},\quad W_{t}=\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{work}}. (3)

A memory context is formed by composing multiple memory contents to support action selection. The function Γ\Gamma defines the step-specific memory context XtX_{t}, which the foundation model uses together with the observation and task goal to generate an action ata_{t}:

Xt=Γ(Dt,Pt,Wt),at∼Fθ(⋅∣Xt,ot,g).X_{t}=\Gamma(D_{t},P_{t},W_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\sim F_{\theta}(\cdot\mid X_{t},o_{t},g). (4)

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the distribution of tasks encountered by the agent. Across decision steps, XtX_{t} may change as memory contents are inserted, evicted, reordered, or associated with different procedural adapters. Let Π\Pi denote a serving policy that reconciles the previous KV cache with the current memory context XtX_{t}. Π\Pi determines which KV states are reused or recomputed during action generation. Our objective is to maximize task success while minimizing inference cost:

Π⋆=arg​maxΠ​𝔼τ∼𝒟​[Succ⁡(τ,Π)−λ​∑t=1TCost⁡(Π,Xt−1,Xt)].\Pi^{\star}=\underset{\Pi}{\operatorname{arg\max}}\underset{\tau\sim\mathcal{D}}{\mathbb{E}}\left[\mathrm{Succ}(\tau;\Pi)-\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{Cost}\!\left(\Pi,X_{t-1},X_{t}\right)\right]. (5)

Here, τ\tau denotes a task instance sampled from 𝒟\mathcal{D}, Succ⁡(τ,Π)\mathrm{Succ}(\tau;\Pi) measures whether τ\tau is successfully completed under Π\Pi, Cost⁡(Π,Xt−1,Xt)\mathrm{Cost}(\Pi,X_{t-1},X_{t}) measures the inference computation incurred under Π\Pi when processing the memory context update from Xt−1X_{t-1} to XtX_{t}, and λ\lambda controls the trade-off between task success and inference cost.

4 Method

4.1 Overall Architecture

We present HeMeR, a heterogeneous memory reconciliation framework that enables foundation model-based embodied agents to process changing memory contexts without rebuilding the full KV cache, as illustrated in Figure 2. At each decision step, the agent obtains memory contents from multiple memory modules and composes them into a single memory context, which the foundation model uses together with the current observation and task goal to generate the next action. During interaction, new observations may introduce memory contents, outdated contents may be removed, existing contents may be reordered, and the active procedural adapter may switch. To handle these changes, HeMeR uses a memory schema to anchor each memory content as a typed memory chunk with an associated KV range. It then reconciles memory-content updates through localized cache operations while preserving compatible KV states across procedural adapter switches.

We distinguish three levels of memory representation: memory modules, memory contents, and memory contexts. A memory module stores and retrieves a specific type of information, and each item retrieved at a decision step is a memory content. A memory context is formed by composing multiple memory contents to support action selection. In our setting, the agent uses declarative, procedural, and working memory modules. Declarative memory stores explicit task and environment knowledge, such as object locations, receptacle relations, and task conditions. Procedural memory stores reusable behavioral procedures, instantiated as LoRA adapters in our LRAgent-based implementation [14]. Working memory stores the current interaction state, including recent observations, intermediate decisions, subgoals, and action history.

Rather than treating the composed memory context XtX_{t} defined in Sec. 3 solely as a flat token sequence, HeMeR organizes it as a sequence of memory chunks. Each memory chunk represents a single memory content, with schema-defined metadata linking it to a contiguous KV range after tokenization and encoding. The memory schema records each chunk’s persistent ID, memory module type, semantic role, normalized content, dependency annotation, position, token span, and KV range, as well as its adapter identifier when applicable. This index maps memory-content updates to their corresponding KV ranges, enabling HeMeR to reconcile the KV cache through localized operations on affected ranges. The initial memory context is prefilled as a single causal sequence. At subsequent decision steps, HeMeR prefills newly inserted memory chunks and selectively recomputes affected KV ranges at their positions in the current memory context, recording the resulting KV ranges in the memory schema.

4.2 Chunk-Level KV Reconciliation

Chunk-level KV reconciliation aligns the previous KV cache with the memory contents in XtX_{t}. As the agent progresses, memory contents may be inserted, evicted, or reordered, potentially altering token positions and dependencies in XtX_{t}. Naive KV reuse is therefore unreliable, while rebuilding the full KV cache can introduce redundant computation when many memory contents remain unchanged.

Schema-Guided Reconciliation.

To address this trade-off, HeMeR uses the chunk-level index to compare memory chunks across consecutive decision steps. Chunks in Xt−1X_{t-1} and XtX_{t} are first matched by persistent chunk IDs, regardless of their positions or token spans. Matched chunks are eligible for KV reuse only when their memory module type, semantic role, dependency annotation, normalized content, and adapter identifier (when applicable) agree. Otherwise, their KV ranges are locally recomputed. Given two consecutive memory contexts, HeMeR computes a schema-guided reconciliation plan

Δt=Diff𝒮​(Xt−1,Xt),\Delta_{t}=\mathrm{Diff}_{\mathcal{S}}(X_{t-1},X_{t}), (6)

where Diff𝒮\mathrm{Diff}_{\mathcal{S}} matches chunks by persistent IDs and checks schema compatibility. Matched chunks with changed positions are reordered, chunks only in XtX_{t} are inserted, and chunks only in Xt−1X_{t-1} are evicted. The index maps these operations to KV ranges, so HeMeR updates only affected ranges.

KV Operations and RoPE Remapping.

Based on the reconciliation plan Δt\Delta_{t}, HeMeR performs the corresponding KV operations. New memory chunks are prefilled, while the KV ranges of evicted chunks are removed. When chunks are reordered, HeMeR relocates their KV ranges according to the current XtX_{t}, reusing compatible KV states when possible. These operations allow the KV cache to be updated without full recomputation.

RoPE remapping is used only for matched chunks whose update is a position shift. If a reusable token shifts from position pjp_{j} to pj′p^{\prime}_{j}, its cached key is updated as

k~j=Rθ⁡(pj′)​Rθ⁡(pj)−1​kj,\tilde{k}_{j}=R_{\theta(p^{\prime}_{j})}R_{\theta(p_{j})}^{-1}k_{j}, (7)

where kjk_{j} denotes the cached key at position pjp_{j}, Rθ⁡(p)R_{\theta(p)} denotes the RoPE rotation at position pp, and k~j\tilde{k}_{j} denotes the remapped key at position pj′p^{\prime}_{j}. This corrects the cached key’s positional phase under a pure position shift. RoPE remapping updates only the cached keys. For multimodal backbones, we restrict RoPE-based remapping to text-side memory chunks whose schema fields remain unchanged [pos:rope]. Visual tokens from current observations are not position-remapped and are encoded normally at each decision step. When content, dependencies, or adapters change, HeMeR recomputes the affected KV range to avoid stale reuse.

Chunk-level KV reconciliation differs from prompt-level or segment-level cache reuse. Prefix caching reuses only stable prefixes, Prompt Cache reuses segments computed without their preceding context, and CacheBlend-style reuse still relies on reusable segment boundaries and selective recomputation around them [serve:cacheblend, serve:kvlink, kv:promptcache]. HeMeR makes the same class of non-prefix reuse approximation, but grounds it in schema-indexed memory chunks and reuses a KV range only when the corresponding memory content remains schema-compatible. Thus, HeMeR avoids both naive KV reuse and full KV cache recomputation by selectively reconciling KV ranges affected by memory-content updates across decision steps.

4.3 Adapter-Stable KV Reconciliation

Procedural memory introduces a second source of cache incompatibility. In our LRAgent-based implementation, procedural memory contents correspond to reusable behavioral procedures implemented as LoRA adapters. When the procedural memory content changes across decision steps, the active adapter may also change. Even if declarative and working-memory contents remain unchanged, KV states computed under the previous adapter may no longer be compatible with the new adapter configuration. This issue is particularly important in embodied tasks, where agents switch among procedures such as searching, manipulating, cleaning, heating, cooling, and placing objects.

Adapter-Aware Reconciliation.

HeMeR maintains adapter identifiers as part of the chunk-level index. For each procedural memory chunk, the index records the adapter under which its KV states were computed, and the reconciliation plan marks adapter switches as procedural updates. When the active adapter changes, HeMeR recomputes the procedural memory chunk’s KV range and those of its direct and transitive dependents under the declared dependency annotations. Other unchanged ranges are approximately reused under the shared-attention LoRA design. This allows adapter switches to be handled within the same indexed reconciliation process without rebuilding the full KV cache.

Cross-Adapter KV Compatibility.

To stabilize cross-adapter reuse, HeMeR adopts the shared-attention LoRA design used by LRAgent. The rank-8 adapters are applied to the query and value projections, with a low-rank down-projection shared across adapters and adapter-specific up-projections. The key, output, and MLP paths remain shared, and the active adapter is applied to the entire forward sequence rather than only to procedural-memory tokens. This design limits, but does not eliminate, cross-adapter drift. Therefore, HeMeR includes the adapter identifier in its KV compatibility condition and recomputes the procedural memory chunk’s KV range while preserving ranges that remain compatible across the switch.

While LRAgent primarily addresses KV cache reuse across adapter switches, HeMeR incorporates adapter compatibility into the same reconciliation process used for updates to declarative and working memory contents. Such methods reduce overhead for procedural changes, but they do not explicitly address updates to declarative and working memory contents that arise during embodied interaction. HeMeR jointly handles both sources of change: adapter switches from procedural memory and chunk-level reconciliation of updates to declarative and working-memory contents. Consequently, HeMeR preserves compatible KV states across heterogeneous memory-content updates while avoiding the need to rebuild the full KV cache at every decision step.

5 Evaluation

5.1 Experimental setting

Environment.

We evaluate on ALFWorld [19], EmbodiedBench Habitat [ben:embodiedbench, 20], and Real-world, a UR7e manipulation setup. Each evaluation episode is unseen in the sense that no single memory fragment covers the required procedure-room combination. Solving these tasks therefore requires composing fragmented memories across different situations rather than retrieving a directly applicable past experience. Real-world evaluation comprises two long-horizon tasks in two tabletop environments, with five independent physical repetitions per task, yielding 10 trials per method. Initial object positions and instruction phrasings vary across repetitions. Benchmark configurations, task details, and evaluation procedures are provided in Appendix A.

Model.

We use two backbone models matched to the observation modality of each environment. For ALFWorld, a text-based environment, we use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct [2]. For EmbodiedBench Habitat, a vision-based 3D environment, we use Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct [3], which natively processes RGB observations. Both are served with greedy decoding (temperature= 0\,{=}\,0). For procedural memory, we use rank-8 LoRA adapters [11] fine-tuned on task-type-specific trajectories for each backbone. Each procedural memory content is linked to an adapter identifier used for adapter selection and KV compatibility checking, as described in Sec. 4.3.

Baselines.

We compare HeMeR with six baselines covering agent-level reasoning, memory use, KV reuse, and procedural adapter switching. ReAct [base:react] tests prompting without explicit external memory, and Reflexion [embodied:reflexion] tests self-reflective feedback from prior failures. MemRL [26] retrieves episodic memory from previous trajectories to guide action selection, but treats the retrieved context as a conventional input across decision steps. CacheBlend [serve:cacheblend] and KEEP [23] evaluate segment-level and invalidation-based KV reuse, respectively. LRAgent [14] tests LoRA-based procedural skill switching, but does not explicitly track updates in declarative or working-memory contents. Together, these baselines separate the effects of prompting, episodic memory retrieval, cache reuse, procedural adapter switching, and the proposed heterogeneous-memory KV reconciliation.

Metrics.

We evaluate task performance, action behavior, and inference efficiency with six metrics. SR measures binary end-to-end task success in ALFWorld and Habitat [19, 20], and goal-conditioned success rate in real-world tasks. Latency measures average wall-clock time per decision step, while TTFT isolates prefill and cache-processing latency before the first generated token, a common serving-level efficiency metric [serve:vllm, serve:cacheblend]. Reuse ratio measures the fraction of KV states preserved after memory-content updates, following prior cache reuse studies [serve:cacheblend, 12]. Active action ratio measures the fraction of generated actions belonging to predefined task-progressing action categories [18]. Action diversity measures the average per-episode ratio of unique actions among all generated actions [4]. In the tables, active ratio and diversity ratio denote active action ratio and action diversity ratio, respectively.

5.2 Main result

Table 1 reports the main results on ALFWorld and Habitat. Across both benchmarks, HeMeR achieves the highest task success while also reducing per-step inference time and improving memory utilization. On ALFWorld, HeMeR reaches 71.43%71.43\% SR with 0.180.18 seconds per step, outperforming the strongest baseline MemRL at 52.86%52.86\% SR with 0.900.90 seconds per step. On Habitat, HeMeR achieves 76.27%76.27\% SR with 1.821.82 seconds per step, improving over MemRL at 61.80%61.80\% SR with 2.682.68 seconds per step. These gains indicate that reconciling dynamically updated memory contents with reusable KV states provides a more effective and efficient decision context than using episodic traces, reactive prompting, or adapter switching in isolation.

The efficiency and memory behavior metrics explain this trend. Although CacheBlend, KEEP, and LRAgent reuse KV states, their reuse ratios remain lower than HeMeR because they do not jointly handle memory-content updates and procedural adapter changes. CacheBlend relies on non-prefix segments, KEEP invalidates affected memory regions, and LRAgent supports procedural LoRA switching without explicitly processing updates to declarative and working-memory contents. In contrast, HeMeR preserves more KV states by indexing memory chunks, updating only affected KV ranges, and maintaining adapter-compatible KV states. Higher active action ratio and action diversity indicate a higher fraction of actions in task-progressing categories and a higher fraction of unique actions. Together, these results show that HeMeR improves long-horizon embodied inference through memory-aware KV reconciliation without rebuilding the full KV cache.

Table 2 reports real-world embodied task results. We focus on MemRL, CacheBlend, KEEP, and LRAgent because they cover the most relevant memory- and cache-specific mechanisms while limiting costly physical robot trials. HeMeR achieves the highest SR, outperforming MemRL by 18.9218.92 percentage points, and reduces inference time from 2.942.94 to 1.871.87 seconds per step. This shows that KV reconciliation remains effective when real-world task progress changes action-relevant memory contents. CacheBlend and LRAgent preserve part of the cache but achieve lower SR, while KEEP improves SR at the cost of lower reuse and higher latency. By contrast, HeMeR achieves the highest KV reuse ratio, active action ratio, and action diversity, indicating stronger cache preservation and action-level behavior.

5.3 Analysis

Cost efficiency under memory-content updates.

Figure 3(a, b) evaluates cost efficiency as the memory context becomes longer and more frequently invalidated. Figure 3(a) varies the number of memory chunks in the memory context, while Figure 3(b) varies the invalidated memory ratio ρ\rho, defined as the fraction of memory chunks affected between consecutive action decisions. Full Rebuild shows the steepest TTFT growth because it recomputes the full memory context at every step. CacheBlend, KEEP, and LRAgent reduce this cost partially, but their gains are limited by narrower reuse assumptions. CacheBlend depends on reusable non-prefix segments, KEEP relies on invalidating affected memory regions, and LRAgent mainly handles procedural LoRA switching without explicitly reconciling updates to declarative and working-memory contents.

In contrast, HeMeR achieves the lowest TTFT by localizing memory-content updates to affected KV ranges and preserving matched chunks through RoPE-based remapping. The reuse-ratio results explain this trend. Baselines rapidly lose reusable cache regions as the invalidated memory ratio increases, whereas HeMeR maintains roughly 1.8×1.8\times higher average reuse and retains more than half of its initial reuse at the largest invalidation ratio. These results reflect the interdependent roles of our components. The memory schema identifies affected regions induced by memory-content updates, chunk-level KV reconciliation preserves positional consistency under insertion, eviction, and reordering, and adapter-stable KV reconciliation supports procedural switches. Together, they enable efficient KV reconciliation without full cache reconstruction.

Operation-level cost decomposition.

Table 3 decomposes cache-processing cost by reconciliation operation, replaying the sequences of memory-content updates collected from ALFWorld episodes, where the reconciliation plan Δt\Delta_{t} maps each update to insertion, eviction, reordering, recomputation, or reuse. Most of the memory context remains reusable across decision steps: 78.3%78.3\% of the processed tokens are reused and 7.9%7.9\% are relocated with RoPE-based remapping, both without recomputation, while only 4,2194{,}219 tokens, 5.6%5.6\% of the 74,78474{,}784 tokens that Full Rebuild recomputes over the same updates, are recomputed. Because insertion and eviction costs are identical to Full Rebuild by construction, the entire reduction in cache-processing time, from 199.4199.4 to 25.825.8 seconds, comes from recomputation avoided on schema-compatible KV ranges. Assembling the reconciled KV cache KtK_{t} adds only 0.5 seconds in total, indicating low cache-assembly overhead relative to recomputation. Note that the reuse ratio in Table 1 is a per-step average over episodes, whereas the token counts here aggregate all replayed memory-content updates.

Further analysis in Appendix C.2 evaluates scalability under increasing memory chunk counts and dependency density, as well as the memory footprint and switching overhead of procedural adapters. Appendix C.2 further decomposes per-step inference latency, showing that the reduction in local memory-context recomputation accounts for most of the observed TTFT improvement.

5.4 Ablation

Table 4 ablates the main components of HeMeR. Removing the memory schema decreases SR from 71.43%71.43\% to 62.67%62.67\% and reuse from 75.30%75.30\% to 51.39%51.39\%. This shows that anchoring memory contents as typed chunks with KV ranges is necessary for identifying which contents remain reusable after memory-content updates. Without this schema, the model cannot reliably map memory contents to affected KV ranges, leading to lower reuse, higher latency, and a lower active action ratio.

Removing chunk-level KV reconciliation causes the largest degradation, reducing SR to 59.40%59.40\% and reuse to 42.75%42.75\%, while increasing latency to 0.470.47 seconds per step. This indicates that the reconciliation plan is the main mechanism for localizing memory-content updates. When chunk-level reconciliation is removed, insertions, evictions, and reorderings can no longer be handled by updating only affected KV ranges, forcing broader recomputation and making cache reuse less stable.

Removing adapter-stable KV reconciliation also degrades performance, but differently. The reuse ratio remains high at 66.40%66.40\%, yet SR drops to 64.85%64.85\% and latency increases to 0.280.28 seconds per step. This suggests that reusing many KV states is insufficient when procedural memory changes the active adapter. Without adapter-stable reconciliation, KV states computed under a previous adapter can become incompatible with the current procedural configuration, reducing decision quality even when cache reuse is preserved. Overall, the ablation results show that the memory schema identifies reusable contents, chunk-level reconciliation localizes memory-content updates, and adapter-stable reconciliation ensures reused states remain compatible under procedural changes.

6 Conclusion

We presented HeMeR, a heterogeneous memory reconciliation framework for foundation model-based embodied agents. HeMeR anchors memory contents as typed memory chunks with associated KV ranges and reconciles memory-content updates through localized KV operations. By combining chunk-level and adapter-stable KV reconciliation, it preserves compatible KV states across changes to declarative, procedural, and working memory contents without rebuilding the full KV cache. Experiments on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world tabletop manipulation tasks show that HeMeR improves task success and reduces per-step inference time over strong baselines. These results demonstrate that reconciling dynamically updated memory contexts with reusable KV states supports efficient and stable inference in long-horizon embodied tasks.

Limitation and future work.

Our evaluation focuses on single-agent embodied tasks, where memory contexts are updated across successive decision steps. In multi-agent embodied systems, concurrent updates to shared memory contents may introduce consistency issues between memory contexts and cached KV states, which are not addressed by the current framework. As future work, we plan to extend HeMeR to multi-agent embodied systems by incorporating concurrency control for shared memory updates and KV reuse. This extension may support efficient memory reconciliation across agents while preserving valid KV states under concurrent updates.
